**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 100, verses 1–2:**

Surat "al-'Adiyat" (The Chargers). It is Meccan according to Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir, al-Hasan, Ikrimah and 'Ata'. It is Medinan according to Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, Malik and Qatadah. It has eleven verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

By the chargers, panting (1), and those that strike sparks of fire (2).

His saying, Most High: ﴿By the chargers, panting﴾, means the horses that run. This is what most of the exegetes (mufassirun) and the people of language (ahl al-lughah) said: they run in the way of Allah, so they pant. Qatadah said: "They pant when they run," meaning they snort (tahmhamah). Al-Farra' said: "al-Dabh (panting) is the sound of the breaths of horses when they run." Ibn 'Abbas said: "No animal pants except the horse, the dog and the fox." It was also said: they were muzzled (yuka'am) with something placed on the mouth of the camel, lest they neigh and the enemy learn of them, so they breathed forcefully in this state. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Allah swore by Muhammad (ﷺ) when He said: ﴿Ya-Sin. By the wise Qur'an﴾ [Ya-Sin: 1–2], and He swore by his life when He said: ﴿By your life, they were wandering blindly in their intoxication﴾ [al-Hijr: 72], and He swore by His horses, their neighing, their dust, and the striking of their hooves against the stone, producing fire, when He said: ﴿By the chargers, panting…﴾, the five verses (following). The people of language said:

*And a stab, with a gushing, flowing wound,*
*I struck it at the chests of the chargers.*

He means the horses. Another said:

*And the chargers, with trails of blood upon them,*
*As if their necks were the stones of sacrifice (tarhib).*

[The verse is by Salamah ibn Jandal. al-Asabi: the streaks of blood; asabi al-dima': its tracks. al-Tarhib: that a tree is propped up when its fruit is heavy, so that its branches do not break. Ibn Manzur said: "He likened the necks of the horses to the prop (al-marhab). It was also said he likened their necks to the stones upon which sacrifices are slaughtered."]

He means the horses. 'Antarah said:

*And the horses are known when they pant*
*In the pools of death, panting.*

Another said:

*I am not the Tubba' of Yemen, if*
*The horses do not pant in the black land of Iraq.*

The people of language said: The original meaning of al-dabh and al-dubah is for foxes, and it was borrowed for horses. It comes from the Arabs' saying: "The fire scorched him (dabahathu al-nar)" when it changed his colour without thoroughly burning him. A poet said:

*So when we roasted a meat that was undercooked (mulhawaj), with its flames blazing (al-lahaban), overpowered and scorched (dabihan)…*

[The verse is by Mudarris al-Asadi. al-Mulhawaj of roasted meat: that which is not fully cooked. al-Lahaban: the kindling and blazing of fire.]

And "inbadaha lawnuhu" means: his colour changed slightly towards blackness. He said:

*I was enamoured of her before the change of my colour (inbidah lawni).*

These animals pant when their condition changes from fear, fatigue or greed. The word ﴿ḍabḥan﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: "and the chargers pant, panting." Al-dabḥ (dabḥ) also means ash (ramad). [In al-Qamus: "al-Dabh, with a kasra, is ash."] The Basrans said: ﴿ḍabḥan﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥal). It was also said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "The horses panted (ḍabaḥat al-khayl ḍabḥan), like ḍabaʿat, which means running." Abu 'Ubaydah also said: "al-Ḍabḥ and al-Ḍabʿ mean running and walking." Likewise al-Mubarrad said: "al-Ḍabḥ is the extension of their forelegs (aḍbaʿ) in motion."

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a detachment (sariyyah) to some people of Banu Kinanah, and news of them was delayed. He had appointed over them al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr al-Ansari, who was one of the nuqaba' (leaders of the pledge). The hypocrites said: "They have been killed." So this surah was revealed to inform the Prophet (ﷺ) of their safety, and as good news to him of their raid upon the people to whom he had sent them. Among those who said that the meaning of al-'Adiyat is the horses are Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, al-Hasan and Mujahid. The intended horses are those on which the believers fight. In a report: "Whoever does not recognise the sanctity of the warrior's horse has a branch of hypocrisy in him."

A second view: they are the camels. Muslim said: "I disputed about this with Ikrimah, and Ikrimah said: 'Ibn 'Abbas said they are the horses.' I said: ''Ali said they are the camels in the Hajj, and my client (mawla) knows better than your client.'" al-Sha'bi said: "'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas disputed about al-'Adiyat. 'Ali said: 'They are the camels running in the Hajj.' Ibn 'Abbas said: 'They are the horses. Do you not see that He says ﴿and raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 4]? Do they raise dust except with their hooves? And do camels pant?'" 'Ali said: "It is not as you say. We saw ourselves on the day of Badr, and with us there was only a dappled horse belonging to al-Miqdad, and a horse belonging to Marthad ibn Abi Marthad. Then 'Ali said to him: 'Do you give fatwas to the people about what you do not know? By Allah, it was the first raid in Islam, and with us were only two horses: a horse for al-Miqdad and a horse for al-Zubayr. So how can al-'Adiyat be panting? Rather, al-'Adiyat are the camels from 'Arafah to Muzdalifah, and from Muzdalifah to 'Arafah.'" Ibn 'Abbas said: "I returned to the view of 'Ali," and Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Suddi also said this.

From this is the saying of Safiyyah bint 'Abd al-Muttalib:

*So, by the chargers at the morning of the gathering,*
*Their forelegs, when the dust rises…*

She means the camels. Those that are called al-'Adiyat are so named from their derivation from al-'adw, which is the spreading of the feet in swift walking. Another said:

*My companion saw in the chargers a noble she-camel,*
*And others like her among the wadiyat (grazing) qawamis.*

[In al-Lisan, under 'd-w: "al-Azhari related from Ibn al-Sikkit: '(Wabil 'adiyah: grazing the fresh pasture and not the saltwort)…'" and he recited the verse. In al-Lisan also, under r-d-ʿ: "Wa-naqah wadiʿah and nuq wadiʿat: grazing the saltwort around the water." Ibn Barri recited the poet's verse… The word "al-qawamis" is thus in al-Lisan and the Sharh al-Qamus, and some copies of the original. In one copy it is "al-qaramis" with a raʾ. The correct reading is probably "al-ʿaramis", the plural of ʿarmas (with kasra on the ʿayn): a hard, strong she-camel.]

As for those who said they are the camels, their saying ḍabḥan means ḍabʿan, and the ḥāʾ according to them is substituted for the ʿayn, because it is said: "ḍabaʿat al-ibil," which is when they extend their necks in motion. al-Mubarrad said: "al-Ḍabʿ is the extension of their forelegs in motion. al-Ḍabḥ is mostly used for horses, and al-Ḍabʿ for camels. The ḥāʾ is sometimes substituted for the ʿayn." Abu Salih said: "al-Ḍabḥ from horses is neighing (ḥamḥamah), and from camels it is breathing." 'Ata' said: "No animal pants except the horse, the fox and the dog, and this is related from Ibn 'Abbas." It has already been mentioned from the people of language that the Arabs say: "The fox panted (ḍabaḥa al-thaʿlab)," and they also use "ḍabaḥa" in other than that. Tawbah said:

*Even if Layla al-Akhyaliyyah had greeted me,*
*While between me and her was dust and stones (jandal)…*

[In one copy: "jandal". This is the reading of the verse.]

*I would have returned the greeting with the warmth of cheerfulness, or an echo from the side of the grave answering her, panting (ḍaʾiḥ).*

[In another narration: "ṣāʾiḥ" (crying out). There is no evidence in it.]

*Zaqa al-ṣadā yazqū zuqāʾan*: that is, it cried out. Every zaqi is a crier, and al-zaqyah is a cry.

**"By those that strike sparks of fire"** (fa-l-muriyāt qadḥan). Ikrimah, 'Ata' and al-Ḍaḥḥak said: "They are the horses when they strike fire with their hooves, and they are the hoofs themselves (sanabik)." This is related from Ibn 'Abbas. And from him also: "They struck with their hooves dust (ghubar)." This contradicts the rest of what is related from him about striking sparks, and this (dust) is about the camels. Ibn Najih related from Mujahid, "wa-l-ʿādiyāti ḍabḥan. Fa-l-mūriyāti qadḥan", he said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is in fighting, and it is in the Hajj." Ibn Mas'ud said: "They are the camels treading on pebbles, so fire comes out of them."

The root of qadḥ is extraction (istikhrāj). From it: "qadaḥtu al-ʿayn," when I extracted from it the corrupt water. And "iqtadaḥtu bi-l-zand," I struck with the firestick. And "iqtadaḥtu al-maraq," I ladled out the broth. A "rakiyy qadūḥ" is a well from which water is scooped by hand. And al-qadīḥ is what remains at the bottom of the pot, which is scooped out with difficulty. Al-miqdaḥah is that with which fire is struck. And al-qaddāḥah and al-qaddāḥ are the stone that produces fire. It is said: "warā al-zand (with a fatḥah) yarī warīan," when its fire came out. There is another dialect: "warī al-zand (with a kasrah) yarī," in both forms. This has already passed in Surat al-Waqi'ah [see vol. 17, p. 221].

*Qadḥan* is in the accusative by the same thing that makes *ḍabḥan* accusative. It was said: these verses are about horses, but their striking fire means that they stir up war between their riders and their enemy. From this it is said of war when it becomes fierce: "ḥamiya al-waṭīs" (the furnace has become hot). From this is His saying, Most High: ﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64]. Its meaning is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah said it. Also from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah said it, and also from Ibn 'Abbas: "The intended meaning of al-muriyat qadḥan is the cunning (makr) of men in war," and Mujahid and Zayd ibn Aslam said this. The Arabs say when a man wants to deceive his companion: "By Allah, I will deceive you, then I will strike fire for you (la-ūriyanna laka)." And from Ibn 'Abbas also: "They are those who raid and kindle their fires at night for their needs and their food." And from him also: "They are the fires of the fighters when their fire is great, to terrify (irhāban). Everyone close to the enemy kindles many fires so that the enemy thinks them many." So this is an oath by that. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "It is the fire that is gathered." It was also said: "They are the thoughts of men that kindle the fire of deceit and treachery." Ikrimah said: "They are the tongues of men that strike fire from the great things they say, and which become manifest through them, such as establishing proofs, establishing evidence, clarifying the truth and nullifying falsehood." Ibn Jurayj related from some of them: "al-Munjihat amran wa-'amalan (those that succeed in matter and deed), like the success of the firestick when it is struck." I say: these sayings are figurative (majaz), and from it is their saying: "So-and-so kindles the sparks of error (zinad al-dalalah)." The first view is the literal meaning (haqiqah): that horses, from the intensity of their running, strike fire with their hooves. Muqatil said: "The Arabs call that fire the fire of Abu Hubahib, and Abu Hubahib was a shaykh of Mudar in the Jahiliyyah, one of the stingiest of people. He would not kindle a fire for bread or anything else until the eyes slept, and then he would kindle a little fire that flares once and dies out another time. If anyone awoke to it, he would put it out, out of dislike that anyone should benefit from it. So the Arabs likened this fire to his fire, because no one benefits from it. Likewise, when the sword strikes the helmet and sparks fire, they call it that." Al-Nabigha said:

*And there is no fault in them, except that their swords*
*Are notched by the clashing of the battalions.*

*They cut through the coat of mail (salawqi), its weaving doubled,*
*And with the blades they kindle the fire of Abu Hubahib.*

[al-Salawqi: a coat of mail attributed to Salawq, a village in Yemen. al-Sifah (sg. safahah): a broad stone.]

From this comes God's words: ﴿So evil is the morning of those who were warned﴾ [al-Saffat: 177]. It was also said: because of their might, they raided by day, and "dawn" (subh) here means openly, likened to the appearance of the dawn. Ibn Mas'ud and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it refers to camels pushed on by their riders on the Day of Sacrifice from Mina to Jam'. The sunnah is that they are not pushed on until morning. Al-Qurtubi also said this. The ighara (raid) is the speed of travel, and from it comes their saying: "Enter the sunrise, Thabir, so that we may raid."[[Thabir: a mountain near Makkah, on the right of one going to 'Arafah. That is, enter into sunrise, which is the light of the sun.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 100, verse 4:

﴿So they raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾ (naq'an), i.e., ghubaran (dust). It means the horses raise dust by the intensity of their running in the place where they made the raid. 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah said:

"I have lost my little daughter if you do not see her... stirring up dust from the two sides of Kada'" [[Kada' (with a fathah on the kaf and a long vowel on the dal): a mountain in Makkah. The pronoun in "tarawha" refers back to the horses, which is understood from the context. The version of the first half of the verse in al-Shawkani 5/469 is: "We have lost our horses..."]]

The pronoun in "bihi" (thereby) refers to the place, or to the location where the raid takes place. When the meaning is known, it is permissible to refer by pronoun to something that has not been explicitly mentioned, as in His words, ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾ [[Verse 32 of Surah Sad.]] [Sad: 32]. It is also said: ﴿fa-atharna bihi﴾ means "by the running" (bil-'adw), ﴿naq'an﴾. The running has already been mentioned. It is also said: al-naq': what lies between Muzdalifah and Mina, as related by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. It is also said: it is the path of the valley, and perhaps it returns to the dust raised from this place.

In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari): al-naq' is dust, and its plural is niqa'. Al-naq' is also the place where water is held back, and likewise what gathers in a well from it. In a hadith: he forbade that the water of a well be withheld (naq' al-bi'r). Al-naq' is also soft, clay-rich ground in which water collects and stands, and its plurals are niqa' and anqu', like bahr, bihar and abhur. I say: al-naq' may also mean raising the voice, and from it is the hadith of 'Umar when it was said to him: "The women have gathered, weeping for Khalid ibn al-Walid." He said: "What is it to the women of Banu al-Mughirah if they shed some of their tears while sitting over Abu Sulayman, so long as there is no naq' and no laqlaqah?" Abu 'Ubayd said: by naq' he means raising the voice; this is the view I have seen among most scholars. From it is the saying of Labid:

"So when a true cry is raised (yanqa' surakh sadiq), they milk them (yuhlibuha), possessing sound and clamour."

It is also reported as "yahlibuha". He means: when they hear a cry, they milk the war, i.e., they gather for it. His words "yanqa' surakh" mean raising the voice. Al-Kisa'i said: his words "naq' wa la laqlaqah": al-naq' is the preparation of food, i.e., at a funeral gathering. From it one says: naqa'tu anqa'u naq'an. Abu 'Ubayd said: he meant by naq' the naqi'ah (a feast), whereas the naqi'ah according to other scholars is the preparation of food upon returning from a journey, not at a funeral. Some said: 'Umar meant by naq' the placing of dust on the head, going by the view that naq' is dust. I do not think 'Umar meant this, nor did he fear it from them, and how could his fear reach that when he disliked for them to stand? So he said: "they shed some of their tears while sitting." Some said: naq' is the tearing of garments (shaq al-juyub), but I do not know what this is in the hadith, nor do I recognise it; in my view naq' in the hadith is only a loud voice, and as for laqlaqah, it is intense loudness, and I have not heard any disagreement about it.

Abu Haywah read ﴿fa-assarna﴾ with shaddah, meaning they made the traces of that. Whoever reads it without shaddah, it is from athara: when he stirs up, and from it ﴿and they stirred up the earth﴾ [[Verse 9 of Surah al-Rum.]] [al-Rum: 9].

Jam'an (جَمْعاً) is the direct object (maf'ul bihi) of fawasatna (فَوَسَطْنَ), meaning: they penetrated with their riders into the enemy, that is, the host (al-jam') which they had raided.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "fawasatna bihi jam'an" means Muzdalifah, and it was called jam' because people gather in it.

It is said: wasatu al-qawma (وَسَطْتُ الْقَوْمَ), asituhum, wasTan, wasiTatan, meaning I came to be in their midst.

Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, read it as (fawassatna) with the doubled letter (tashdid). This is the reading of Qatadah, Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Raja'. The two are dialectal variants (lughatan) with the same meaning: wasatu al-qawma (with tashdid and with takhfif) and tawassatahum mean one and the same thing. It is also said that the meaning of tashdid is making it (the jam') into two parts, while takhfif means they were in the middle of the host. Both return to the meaning of the host (al-jam').

This is the answer to the oath: that man has been created prone to ingratitude for blessings. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Lakanud" means truly ungrateful and denying of the blessings of Allah. Al-Hasan said the same, and added: he mentions calamities and forgets blessings. A poet took this and versified it:

O you who are unjust in his deed... and injustice is returned upon the one who did wrong,
How long will you, and until when, complain of misfortunes and forget blessings!

Abu Umamah al-Bahili narrated, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The kanud is the one who eats alone, withholds his largesse (rifd) [[al-rifd (with a kasra on the ra): gift and kindness.]], and beats his servant." And Ibn 'Abbas narrated, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I inform you of your worst?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "The one who dwells alone, withholds his largesse, and flogs his servant." Both were narrated by al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim in Nawadir al-Usul.

It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Kanud" in the language of Kindah and Hadramawt means the disobedient; in the language of Rabi'ah and Mudar it means the ungrateful; and in the language of Kinanah it means the stingy, of bad disposition. Muqatil also said this. A poet said:

Kanud to the favours of men, and whoever is kanud to the favours of men will be distanced.

That is, ungrateful. It was said: it is one who disbelieves over little and does not give thanks for much. It was said: it is one who denies the truth. It was said: Kindah was named Kindah only because it denied its father. Ibrahim ibn Harmah the poet said:

Leave the misers if they grow haughty and turn away, and the mention of the stinginess of a kanud coquette.

It was also said: al-kanud is from kanada, meaning he cut off, as if he cuts off what he should maintain of gratitude. It is said: kanada al-habl, meaning he cut the rope. Al-A'sha said:

Withdraw [[maTa al-adha maytan wa amatahu: he removed it and buried it. He means: if you turn away from me, I am firm of heart and joined to whoever joins, ungrateful to whoever is ungrateful. The version of the first half of the verse is in al-Lisan. Fa-mitai means: withdraw and go away.]] you withdraw, with a firm heart, joining with ropes and cutting them off.

This indicates cutting. It is said: kanada yaknudu kunudan, meaning he denied the blessing and rejected it, so he is kanud. A woman may also be kanud, and kanad is similar. Al-A'sha said:

Renew for her, she renews for your union; indeed she is kanud to the union of the frequent visitor.

That is, ungrateful for reciprocity. Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-insan" here means the disbeliever; he says "indeed he is kanud," and from this comes "the kanud land," which produces nothing. Al-Dahhak said: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. Al-Mubarrad said: al-kanud is the one who withholds what is due upon him. And he recited for Kuthayyir:

Renew for her, she renews for your union; indeed she is kanud to the union of the frequent visitor.

Abu Bakr al-Wasiti said: al-kanud is one who spends Allah's blessings in disobedience to Allah. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: al-kanud is one who sees the blessing as coming from himself and his helpers. Al-Tirmidhi said: one who sees the blessing but does not see the Bestower. Dhu al-Nun al-Misri said: the hala' and the kanud is one who, when evil touches him, is distressed, and when good touches him, withholds. It was said: he is the spiteful, envious one. It was said: he is one who is ignorant of his own worth. In wisdom literature: whoever is ignorant of his own power has torn away his veil.

I say: all these sayings return to the meaning of ingratitude and denial. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained the meaning of al-kanud with blameworthy traits and undesirable states; if it is authentic, then it is the highest thing said, and no one has any further argument against it.

Surah 100, verse 7: "And indeed he is, to that, a witness."

That is, indeed Allah, may His majesty be exalted and His praise be great, is a witness to that from the son of Adam. Thus Mansur narrated from Mujahid, and this is the view of most of the exegetes, and it is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "And indeed he" means that indeed man is a witness against himself by what he does. This was also narrated from Mujahid.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And indeed he﴾, i.e., man, without disagreement.

(For the love of good) i.e., wealth. From this is the words of Allah: "If he leaves behind some good" [footnote: Qur'an 2:180] [Al-Baqarah: 180]. And ʿAdiyy said:

"What do souls hope for in seeking wealth, when the love of life is its gloom?" [footnote: *kāribuhā*: its gloom, from *karaba al-amr*: the matter became severe upon him.]

(Indeed he is severe) i.e., strong in his love of wealth. It was also said: "severe" means stingy. The stingy person is called *shadīd* and *mutashaddid*. Ṭarafa said:

"I see death choosing the noblemen, and selecting the choicest possession of the wicked, stingy one."

It is said: *iʿtamahu* and *iʿtamāhu*, meaning he chose him. *Al-fāḥish* also means the stingy. From this is the words of Allah: "and He commands you to indecency" [footnote: Qur'an 2:268] [Al-Baqarah: 268], i.e., stinginess. Ibn Zayd said: Allah named wealth "good," though it may be evil and unlawful, but people consider it good, so Allah named it good for that reason. Jihad was likewise named in the same way, when He said: "So they returned with a blessing from Allah and grace, no harm touched them" [footnote: Qur'an 3:174] [Āl ʿImrān: 174], according to what people call it. Al-Farrāʾ said: the proper structure of the verse would be: "indeed he is severely loving of good," but when the love was mentioned first, he said "severe," and the mention of love was omitted at the end, because it had already been mentioned, and for the sake of the *ruʾūs al-āy* (the rhyme endings of the verses), like His words: "on a stormy day" [footnote: Qur'an 14:18] [Ibrāhīm: 18]. "Stormy" (*ʿāṣif*) belongs to the wind, not the days, so when the wind was mentioned before the day, the mention of the wind was dropped at the end, as if he had said: "on a day of stormy wind."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 100, verse 9–11:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Does he not know﴾, that is, the son of Adam, ﴿when what is in the graves is scattered﴾, that is, is stirred up, overturned and searched, so that what is in them is brought out. Abu 'Ubayda said: "I scattered the goods (ba'thartu al-mata'): I made their bottom their top." It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b that he said: "That is when they are resurrected." Al-Farra' said: "I heard some of the Bedouins of Banu Asad reading buhthira with a ḥā' in place of the 'ayn," and al-Mawardi related it from Ibn Mas'ud, and both have the same meaning.

﴿And what is in the breasts is made known﴾, that is, what is in them of good and evil is distinguished; so said the commentators. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is brought forth. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Nasr ibn 'Asim read wa-ḥaṣala with a fatḥa on the ḥā' and a light ṣād, and also with a fatḥa on the ṣād, meaning it became apparent.

﴿Indeed, their Lord, that Day, is Acquainted with them﴾, that is, Knowing, nothing of them concealed from Him. He knows them on that day and on other days, but the meaning is that He will recompense them on that day. As for His saying, ﴿when what is in the graves is scattered﴾, the governing element in "idha" is buthira, and yaʿlamu does not govern it, since knowledge by man at that time is not what is intended; rather, it is intended in this world. Nor does lakhabirun govern it, because what follows "inna" does not govern what precedes it. The governing element in yawma'idhin is lakhabirun, even though the lam separates them, because the place of the lam is the beginning (of the sentence); it entered the predicate because inna entered upon the subject.

It is narrated that al-Hajjaj recited this surah from the pulpit urging the people to campaign, and there slipped from his tongue: "anna rabbahum" with a fatḥa on the alif; then he corrected himself and said: "lakhabirun" without the lam. Had it not been for the lam, it would have been fatḥa, because knowledge falls upon it. Abu al-Sammal read: "Anna rabbahum bihim yawma'idhin khabirun."

And Allah, Glorified and Exalted, knows best.
